claim: Social touch constitutes a key component of human social relationships.
source: Social touch constitutes a key component of human social relationships, although in some conditions with social dysfunction, such as autism, it can be perceived as unpleasant.
evidence: This is a general statement about social touch supported by established scientific understanding.

claim: In some conditions with social dysfunction, such as autism, social touch can be perceived as unpleasant.
source: Social touch constitutes a key component of human social relationships, although in some conditions with social dysfunction, such as autism, it can be perceived as unpleasant.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about autism and social touch perception.

claim: Intranasal administration of oxytocin facilitates the pleasantness of social touch and activation of brain reward and social processing regions.
source: We have previously shown that intranasal administration of oxytocin facilitates the pleasantness of social touch and activation of brain reward and social processing regions, although it is unclear if it influences responses to gentle stroking touch mediated by cutaneous C-touch fibers or pressure touch mediated by other types of fibers.
evidence: This claim references previous research by the authors.

claim: Both intranasal and oral oxytocin equivalently enhanced pleasantness ratings for gentle-stroking touch but not medium pressure touch.
source: Although both types of touch were perceived as pleasant, intranasal and oral oxytocin equivalently enhanced pleasantness ratings and responses of reward, orbitofrontal cortex, and social processing, superior temporal sulcus, regions only to gentle-stroking not medium pressure touch.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Both intranasal and oral oxytocin enhanced responses in the orbitofrontal cortex and superior temporal sulcus regions only to gentle-stroking touch, not medium pressure touch.
source: Although both types of touch were perceived as pleasant, intranasal and oral oxytocin equivalently enhanced pleasantness ratings and responses of reward, orbitofrontal cortex, and social processing, superior temporal sulcus, regions only to gentle-stroking not medium pressure touch.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fNIRS neural data collected in the study.

claim: Increased blood oxytocin concentrations predicted the pleasantness of gentle stroking touch.
source: Furthermore, increased blood oxytocin concentrations predicted the pleasantness of gentle stroking touch.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analyses between blood OT concentrations and behavioral ratings.

claim: The specificity of neural effects of oxytocin on C-touch targeted gentle stroking touch were confirmed by time-course extraction and classification analysis.
source: The specificity of neural effects of oxytocin on C-touch targeted gentle stroking touch were confirmed by time-course extraction and classification analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from the classification analysis performed on the neural data.

claim: Increased peripheral concentrations of oxytocin primarily modulate its behavioral and neural responses to gentle social touch mediated by C-touch fibers.
source: Increased peripheral concentrations of oxytocin primarily modulate its behavioral and neural responses to gentle social touch mediated by C-touch fibers.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings comparing intranasal and oral OT administration.

claim: Large myelinated Aβ fibers are densely packed in the fingertips and lips and subserve discriminative touch.
source: While large myelinated Aβ fibers are densely packed in the fingertips and lips and subserve discriminative touch, unmyelinated C-touch (CT) fibers exist in hairy skin and only respond to low force/velocity (caress-like stroking) touch (Croy et al., 2016; McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Unmyelinated C-touch (CT) fibers exist in hairy skin and only respond to low force/velocity (caress-like stroking) touch.
source: While large myelinated Aβ fibers are densely packed in the fingertips and lips and subserve discriminative touch, unmyelinated C-touch (CT) fibers exist in hairy skin and only respond to low force/velocity (caress-like stroking) touch (Croy et al., 2016; McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CT fibers are specialized for the affective domain of touch and have evolved to signal the rewarding value of physical contact.
source: The latter fibers are specialized for the affective domain of touch and have evolved to signal the rewarding value of physical contact (Liljencrantz and Olausson, 2014; Pawling et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Stimulation of the CT system primarily engages the insula via the spinothalamic tract and brain circuits involved in reward and social-emotional information processing such as the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS).
source: Stimulation of the CT system primarily engages the insula via the spinothalamic tract and brain circuits involved in reward and social-emotional information processing such as the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) (Björnsdotter et al., 2014; Davidovic et al., 2016; Gordon et al., 2013; Morrison, 2016; Olausson et al., 2002; Olausson et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Medium pressure touch in the form of hugging or massage can be perceived as pleasant but mainly influences pressure receptors of non-CT fibers.
source: Medium pressure touch in the form of hugging or massage can also be perceived as pleasant but mainly influences pressure receptors of non-CT fibers (Case et al., 2021; Field, 2010) and primarily targets the somatosensory cortex via the spinothalamic tract (McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Medium pressure touch primarily targets the somatosensory cortex via the spinothalamic tract.
source: Medium pressure touch in the form of hugging or massage can also be perceived as pleasant but mainly influences pressure receptors of non-CT fibers (Case et al., 2021; Field, 2010) and primarily targets the somatosensory cortex via the spinothalamic tract (McGlone et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neural substrates of pleasurable gentle stroking and medium pressure touch overlap to some extent but may also involve different parts of the somatosensory cortex and insula.
source: While neural substrates of pleasurable gentle stroking and medium pressure touch overlap to some extent they may also involve different parts of the somatosensory cortex and insula (Case et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The neuropeptide oxytocin (OT) plays a key role in the regulation of social cognition and the rewarding aspects of social stimuli, including social affective touch.
source: The neuropeptide oxytocin (OT) plays a key role in the regulation of social cognition and the rewarding aspects of social stimuli, including social affective touch (Bartz et al., 2011; Kendrick et al., 2017; Rae et al., 2022; Wigton et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: There is a close association between OT and CT-targeted social touch.
source: There is a close association between OT and CT-targeted social touch (Moberg et al., 2020; Uvnäs-Moberg et al., 2014; Walker et al., 2017) and studies have shown that social touch, particularly administered as gentle stroking touch or medium pressure massage, can activate parvocellular oxytocinergic neurons (Okabe et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2020) and facilitate endogenous OT release in the saliva, blood or urine across species (Crockford et al., 2013; Holt-Lunstad et al., 2008; Li et al., 2019; Morhenn et al., 2012; Portnova et al., 2020; Vittner et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Social touch, particularly administered as gentle stroking touch or medium pressure massage, can activate parvocellular oxytocinergic neurons.
source: There is a close association between OT and CT-targeted social touch (Moberg et al., 2020; Uvnäs-Moberg et al., 2014; Walker et al., 2017) and studies have shown that social touch, particularly administered as gentle stroking touch or medium pressure massage, can activate parvocellular oxytocinergic neurons (Okabe et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2020) and facilitate endogenous OT release in the saliva, blood or urine across species (Crockford et al., 2013; Holt-Lunstad et al., 2008; Li et al., 2019; Morhenn et al., 2012; Portnova et al., 2020; Vittner et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Social touch can facilitate endogenous OT release in the saliva, blood or urine across species.
source: There is a close association between OT and CT-targeted social touch (Moberg et al., 2020; Uvnäs-Moberg et al., 2014; Walker et al., 2017) and studies have shown that social touch, particularly administered as gentle stroking touch or medium pressure massage, can activate parvocellular oxytocinergic neurons (Okabe et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2020) and facilitate endogenous OT release in the saliva, blood or urine across species (Crockford et al., 2013; Holt-Lunstad et al., 2008; Li et al., 2019; Morhenn et al., 2012; Portnova et al., 2020; Vittner et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Intranasal OT enhances the perceived pleasantness and activity of the reward system and salience network in response to gentle social touch by a female in men.
source: More specifically, intranasal OT enhances the perceived pleasantness and activity of the reward system and salience network in response to gentle social touch by a female in men (Scheele et al., 2014), by their partners rather than by an unfamiliar female (Kreuder et al., 2017), or during foot massage administered by a human but not by a machine (Chen et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Intranasal OT enhances responses to gentle social touch by partners rather than by an unfamiliar female.
source: More specifically, intranasal OT enhances the perceived pleasantness and activity of the reward system and salience network in response to gentle social touch by a female in men (Scheele et al., 2014), by their partners rather than by an unfamiliar female (Kreuder et al., 2017), or during foot massage administered by a human but not by a machine (Chen et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Intranasal OT enhances responses during foot massage administered by a human but not by a machine.
source: More specifically, intranasal OT enhances the perceived pleasantness and activity of the reward system and salience network in response to gentle social touch by a female in men (Scheele et al., 2014), by their partners rather than by an unfamiliar female (Kreuder et al., 2017), or during foot massage administered by a human but not by a machine (Chen et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Intranasal OT enhances the pleasantness of gentle stroking touch administered indirectly via different materials independent of valence.
source: Intranasal OT also enhances the pleasantness of gentle stroking touch administered indirectly via different materials independent of valence (Chen et al., 2020a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Intranasally administered OT can directly enter the brain via the olfactory and trigeminal nerves.
source: A number of studies have established that intranasally administered OT can directly enter the brain via the olfactory and trigeminal nerves (see Lee et al., 2020; Quintana et al., 2021) and it has been widely assumed to be the main route whereby intranasal OT produces effects on brain and behavior.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Intranasally administered OT enters the peripheral circulation after absorption by nasal and oral blood vessels.
source: However, intranasally administered OT also enters the peripheral circulation after absorption by nasal and oral blood vessels and may produce functional effects by entering the brain after binding to the receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) and crossing the blood brain barrier (BBB; Yamamoto and Higashida, 2020), or by vagal stimulation following stimulation of its receptors in the heart and gastrointestinal system (see Carter, 2014; Carter et al., 2020; Yao and Kendrick, 2022) or following stimulation of receptors in other organs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: OT may produce functional effects by entering the brain after binding to RAGE and crossing the blood brain barrier.
source: However, intranasally administered OT also enters the peripheral circulation after absorption by nasal and oral blood vessels and may produce functional effects by entering the brain after binding to the receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) and crossing the blood brain barrier (BBB; Yamamoto and Higashida, 2020), or by vagal stimulation following stimulation of its receptors in the heart and gastrointestinal system (see Carter, 2014; Carter et al., 2020; Yao and Kendrick, 2022) or following stimulation of receptors in other organs.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: OT may produce functional effects by vagal stimulation following stimulation of its receptors in the heart and gastrointestinal system.
source: However, intranasally administered OT also enters the peripheral circulation after absorption by nasal and oral blood vessels and may produce functional effects by entering the brain after binding to the receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) and crossing the blood brain barrier (BBB; Yamamoto and Higashida, 2020), or by vagal stimulation following stimulation of its receptors in the heart and gastrointestinal system (see Carter, 2014; Carter et al., 2020; Yao and Kendrick, 2022) or following stimulation of receptors in other organs.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: Reducing the entry of oxytocin into the peripheral circulation following intranasal administration using a vasoconstrictor prevents its effects on resting state electroencephalographic changes involving cross-frequency coupling.
source: Indeed, in a recent study we have shown that reducing the entry of oxytocin into the peripheral circulation following intranasal administration using a vasoconstrictor prevents its effects on resting state electroencephalographic changes involving cross-frequency coupling (Yao et al., 2023).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: Peripheral OT could influence OT receptors in keratinocytes in the skin which may act to modulate activity of responses of cutaneous sensory fibers.
source: In the specific context of responses to tactile stimulation peripheral OT could influence OT receptors in keratinocytes in the skin which may act to modulate activity of responses of cutaneous sensory fibers (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Deing et al., 2013; Talagas and Misery, 2019) or in spinal dorsal route ganglion neurons which receive inputs from cutaneous sensory fibers and project to the brain via the spinothalamic tract (González-Hernández et al., 2017; Noguri et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: Peripheral OT could influence OT receptors in spinal dorsal route ganglion neurons which receive inputs from cutaneous sensory fibers and project to the brain via the spinothalamic tract.
source: In the specific context of responses to tactile stimulation peripheral OT could influence OT receptors in keratinocytes in the skin which may act to modulate activity of responses of cutaneous sensory fibers (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Deing et al., 2013; Talagas and Misery, 2019) or in spinal dorsal route ganglion neurons which receive inputs from cutaneous sensory fibers and project to the brain via the spinothalamic tract (González-Hernández et al., 2017; Noguri et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research and represents a proposed mechanism.

claim: Intranasal and oral administration of OT have been shown to produce similar effects on visual attention and state anxiety.
source: Support for peripherally mediated routes have been found in animal model studies reporting functional effects of OT administered subcutaneously or intraperitoneally (see Yao and Kendrick, 2022), and in a previous study, we have shown similar effects of intranasal and oral (lingual) OT on visual attention and state anxiety (Zhuang et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: In monkeys, intranasal and intravenous administration of OT have been reported to produce different patterns of regional perfusion.
source: For example, in monkeys intranasal and intravenous administration of OT have been reported to produce different patterns of regional perfusion (Lee et al., 2018), although in humans they produced similar neural effects (Martins et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In humans, intranasal and intravenous administration of OT produced similar neural effects.
source: For example, in monkeys intranasal and intravenous administration of OT have been reported to produce different patterns of regional perfusion (Lee et al., 2018), although in humans they produced similar neural effects (Martins et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Intranasal and oral (lingual) OT have different effects on amygdala and putamen responses to emotional faces and on associated arousal.
source: Another recent study in humans has shown that intranasal and oral (lingual) OT have different effects on amygdala and putamen responses to emotional faces and on associated arousal (Kou et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A total of 171 subjects (87 females, 21.58±1.94 years) were analyzed in the study.
source: Thus data from a final sample of 171 subjects (87 females, 21.58±1.94 years) were analyzed (intranasal OT: N=56; oral OT: N=57; PLC: N=58) (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample.

claim: There were no significant differences between treatment groups with respect to demographics and questionnaire scores measuring personality traits and mood.
source: Repeated-measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) with treatment as between-subject factor revealed no significant differences between treatment groups (ps >0.130) with respect to demographics and questionnaire scores measuring personality traits and mood (Table 1 and Supplementary file 1 Table 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analyses of demographic and questionnaire data.

claim: There was no between-group difference in basal plasma OT concentrations taken prior to the treatment.
source: A one-way ANOVA showed no between-group difference in basal plasma OT concentrations taken prior to the treatment (F(2, 168)=2.39, p=0.105; Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of baseline blood samples.

claim: Intranasal OT treatment resulted in a mean increase of 6.26 ± 0.93 pg/ml in plasma OT concentrations at 30 min post-treatment compared to placebo.
source: A one-way ANOVA on increases in plasma concentrations relative to basal levels revealed a significant main effect of treatment (F(2, 168)=29.46, p<0.001) with higher plasma OT concentration changes at 30 min (before the task) following intranasal (mean increase = 6.26 ± 0.93 pg/ml, p<0.001) and oral OT treatment (mean increase = 2.10 ± 0.42 pg/ml, p=0.016) compared with PLC (mean increase = –0.31 ± 0.35 pg/ml).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of blood samples.

claim: Oral OT treatment resulted in a mean increase of 2.10 ± 0.42 pg/ml in plasma OT concentrations at 30 min post-treatment compared to placebo.
source: A one-way ANOVA on increases in plasma concentrations relative to basal levels revealed a significant main effect of treatment (F(2, 168)=29.46, p<0.001) with higher plasma OT concentration changes at 30 min (before the task) following intranasal (mean increase = 6.26 ± 0.93 pg/ml, p<0.001) and oral OT treatment (mean increase = 2.10 ± 0.42 pg/ml, p=0.016) compared with PLC (mean increase = –0.31 ± 0.35 pg/ml).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of blood samples.

claim: Plasma OT concentrations following intranasal treatment were significantly higher than following oral treatment.
source: Plasma OT concentrations following intranasal treatment were also significantly higher than following oral treatment (p<0.001, Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1 Table 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of blood samples, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Plasma OT concentrations in the intranasal and oral OT groups following the gentle stroking touch and medium pressure massage were both significantly higher than in the PLC group.
source: To investigate changes of plasma OT concentrations after the gentle stroking touch relative to the medium pressure massage, a repeated-measures ANOVA on plasma OT concentrations measured after each touch stimulation session with treatment as between-subject factor and condition as within-subject factor revealed a significant main effect of treatment (F(2, 166)=14.20, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.15) indicating that plasma OT concentrations in the intranasal (p<0.001) and oral OT groups (p=0.003) following the gentle stroking touch and medium pressure massage were both significantly higher than in the PLC group, whereas no difference was found between intranasal and oral OT treatment groups (p=0.162).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of blood samples taken after touch sessions.

claim: There was no difference in plasma OT concentrations between intranasal and oral OT treatment groups following the touch sessions.
source: To investigate changes of plasma OT concentrations after the gentle stroking touch relative to the medium pressure massage, a repeated-measures ANOVA on plasma OT concentrations measured after each touch stimulation session with treatment as between-subject factor and condition as within-subject factor revealed a significant main effect of treatment (F(2, 166)=14.20, p<0.001, ηp2 = 0.15) indicating that plasma OT concentrations in the intranasal (p<0.001) and oral OT groups (p=0.003) following the gentle stroking touch and medium pressure massage were both significantly higher than in the PLC group, whereas no difference was found between intranasal and oral OT treatment groups (p=0.162).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of blood samples taken after touch sessions.

claim: Plasma OT concentrations were higher following the gentle stroking touch (mean increase: 2.18±0.36 pg/ml) than medium pressure massage (mean increase: 1.67±0.30 pg/ml).
source: There was also a marginal main effect of condition (F(1, 166)=3.39, p=0.067, ηp2 = 0.02), with plasma OT concentrations being higher following the gentle stroking touch (mean increase: 2.18±0.36 pg/ml) than medium pressure massage (mean increase: 1.67±0.30 pg/ml).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of blood samples, though the effect was marginal.

claim: Both intranasal OT and oral OT significantly increased pleasantness ratings of the gentle stroking touch compared with PLC group.
source: Post-hoc Bonferroni corrected tests showed that both intranasal OT (p=0.006) and oral OT (p=0.044) significantly increased pleasantness ratings of the gentle stroking touch compared with PLC group (Figure 2C), but not for the medium pressure massage (ps >0.960) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral rating data, with reference to Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Neither intranasal OT nor oral OT significantly increased pleasantness ratings of the medium pressure massage.
source: Post-hoc Bonferroni corrected tests showed that both intranasal OT (p=0.006) and oral OT (p=0.044) significantly increased pleasantness ratings of the gentle stroking touch compared with PLC group (Figure 2C), but not for the medium pressure massage (ps >0.960) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral rating data, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Subjects rated the medium pressure massage more pleasant than the gentle stroking touch.
source: The main effect of stimulation condition was also significant (F(1, 168)=58.42, p<0.001, ƞp2 = 0.26), with subjects rating the medium pressure massage (6.87±0.08) more pleasant than the gentle stroking touch (5.95±0.11).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral rating data.

claim: Subjects perceived the medium pressure massage as more arousing than the gentle stroking touch.
source: Analyses of other ratings revealed a significant effect of stimulation condition with subjects perceiving the medium pressure massage more arousing (F(1, 168)=44.62, p<0.001, ƞp2 = 0.21), and intense (F(1, 168)=634.83, p<0.001, ƞp2 = 0.79) and being willing to pay more for it (F(1, 168)=91.38, p<0.001, ƞp2 = 0.35) than the gentle stroking touch.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral rating data.

claim: Subjects perceived the medium pressure massage as more intense than the gentle stroking touch.
source: Analyses of other ratings revealed a significant effect of stimulation condition with subjects perceiving the medium pressure massage more arousing (F(1, 168)=44.62, p<0.001, ƞp2 = 0.21), and intense (F(1, 168)=634.83, p<0.001, ƞp2 = 0.79) and being willing to pay more for it (F(1, 168)=91.38, p<0.001, ƞp2 = 0.35) than the gentle stroking touch.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral rating data.

claim: Subjects were willing to pay more for the medium pressure massage than the gentle stroking touch.
source: Analyses of other ratings revealed a significant effect of stimulation condition with subjects perceiving the medium pressure massage more arousing (F(1, 168)=44.62, p<0.001, ƞp2 = 0.21), and intense (F(1, 168)=634.83, p<0.001, ƞp2 = 0.79) and being willing to pay more for it (F(1, 168)=91.38, p<0.001, ƞp2 = 0.35) than the gentle stroking touch.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral rating data.

claim: There were no significant main effects of treatment or interactions for arousal or intensity ratings, or ratings of willingness to pay.
source: There were no significant main effects of treatment or interactions for arousal (ps >0.138) or intensity (ps >0.107) ratings, or ratings of willingness to pay (ps >0.354).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral rating data.

claim: Gender and menstrual cycle did not significantly affect pleasantness ratings.
source: Additional analyses of possible gender and menstrual cycle-dependent effects revealed no significant effects on pleasantness ratings (gender: ps >0.316, menstrual cycle: ps >0.110).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral rating data.

claim: The perceived gender of the masseur did not significantly influence the pleasantness ratings in either of the stimulation conditions or on the effects of OT on increasing pleasantness ratings of gentle stroking touch.
source: Moreover, the perceived gender of the masseur did not significantly influence the pleasantness ratings in either of the stimulation condition (ps >0.441) or on the effects of OT on increasing pleasantness ratings of gentle stroking touch (ps >0.364; see Supplementary file 1 Table 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral rating data.

claim: Both types of touch influenced sympathetic nervous system measures of arousal (increased SCR and heart rate) and parasympathetic measures of vagal tone (increased HRV).
source: Thus, both types of touch influenced sympathetic nervous system measures of arousal (increased SCR and heart rate) and parasympathetic measures of vagal tone (increased HRV), although medium pressure was more potent than gentle stroking touch with the exception of heart rate.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of physiological data.

claim: Medium pressure massage was more potent than gentle stroking touch in influencing autonomic measures, with the exception of heart rate.
source: Thus, both types of touch influenced sympathetic nervous system measures of arousal (increased SCR and heart rate) and parasympathetic measures of vagal tone (increased HRV), although medium pressure was more potent than gentle stroking touch with the exception of heart rate.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of physiological data.

claim: OT treatment did not influence either sympathetic or parasympathetic responses to touch.
source: However, OT treatment did not influence either sympathetic or parasympathetic responses to touch.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of physiological data.

claim: Both intranasal and oral OT significantly enhanced activity in the bilateral mOFC compared with PLC only in response to gentle stroking touch.
source: Post-hoc Bonferroni corrected pair-wise comparisons for each ROI revealed that both intranasal and oral OT significantly enhanced the activity in the bilateral mOFC (intranasal OT: p1=0.029, oral OT: p2=0.005), mlOFC (intranasal OT: p1=0.005, oral OT: p2=0.030) and pSTS (intranasal OT: p1=0.043, oral OT: p2=0.040) compared with the PLC only in response to gentle stroking touch.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of fNIRS neural data.

claim: Both intranasal and oral OT significantly enhanced activity in the bilateral mlOFC compared with PLC only in response to gentle stroking touch.
source: Post-hoc Bonferroni corrected pair-wise comparisons for each ROI revealed that both intranasal and oral OT significantly enhanced the activity in the bilateral mOFC (intranasal OT: p1=0.029, oral OT: p2=0.005), mlOFC (intranasal OT: p1=0.005, oral OT: p2=0.030) and pSTS (intranasal OT: p1=0.043, oral OT: p2=0.040) compared with the PLC only in response to gentle stroking touch.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of fNIRS neural data.

claim: Both intranasal and oral OT significantly enhanced activity in the pSTS compared with PLC only in response to gentle stroking touch.
source: Post-hoc Bonferroni corrected pair-wise comparisons for each ROI revealed that both intranasal and oral OT significantly enhanced the activity in the bilateral mOFC (intranasal OT: p1=0.029, oral OT: p2=0.005), mlOFC (intranasal OT: p1=0.005, oral OT: p2=0.030) and pSTS (intranasal OT: p1=0.043, oral OT: p2=0.040) compared with the PLC only in response to gentle stroking touch.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of fNIRS neural data.

claim: There were no significant treatment effects on neural responses in the lOFC and S1.
source: There were no significant treatment effects on neural responses in the lOFC (ps >0.559) and S1 (ps >0.993).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of fNIRS neural data.

claim: For the medium pressure massage, no significant treatment effects on neural responses were found.
source: For the medium pressure massage, no significant treatment effects were found (ps >0.237) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of fNIRS neural data, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Both intranasal and oral OT prolonged the response in the bilateral mlOFC, mOFC and pSTS to gentle stroking touch.
source: Extraction of time courses of oxy-Hb concentration changes showed distinct hemodynamic patterns in response to medium pressure massage and gentle stroking touch. In comparison with oxy-Hb concentration showing a convergent tendency across intranasal OT, oral OT and PLC groups after offset of the massage stimulation, both intranasal and oral OT prolonged the response in the bilateral mlOFC, mOFC and pSTS to gentle stroking touch (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course analysis of fNIRS neural data, with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Time courses of the mOFC, mlOFC and pSTS could discriminate between intranasal OT and PLC groups with 70.1% accuracy.
source: Results showed that time courses of the mOFC, mlOFC and pSTS could achieve a modest level to discriminate between intranasal OT and PLC (mean accuracy = 70.1%, permutation test p<0.001) and between oral OT and PLC groups (mean accuracy = 64.3%, permutation test p=0.008).
evidence: This is a finding from classification analysis of fNIRS neural data.

claim: Time courses of the mOFC, mlOFC and pSTS could discriminate between oral OT and PLC groups with 64.3% accuracy.
source: Results showed that time courses of the mOFC, mlOFC and pSTS could achieve a modest level to discriminate between intranasal OT and PLC (mean accuracy = 70.1%, permutation test p<0.001) and between oral OT and PLC groups (mean accuracy = 64.3%, permutation test p=0.008).
evidence: This is a finding from classification analysis of fNIRS neural data.

claim: The classification accuracy for discriminating between intranasal and oral OT groups was not significantly higher than chance (mean accuracy = 51.3%).
source: However, the classification accuracy for discriminating between intranasal and oral OT groups was not significantly higher than the classification accuracy on the null distribution (mean accuracy = 51.3%, permutation test p=0.494; see Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from classification analysis of fNIRS neural data, with reference to Figure 5.

claim: Post-treatment OT concentration changes were positively correlated with pleasantness rating scores for gentle stroking touch.
source: Post-treatment OT concentration changes (30 min post-treatment and before task) were found to be positively correlated with pleasantness rating scores (Spearman's rho = 0.18, p=0.017) and oxy-Hb concentration changes in the mlOFC (Spearman's rho = 0.16, p=0.044) in response to the gentle stroking touch.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis between blood OT concentrations and behavioral ratings.

claim: Post-treatment OT concentration changes were positively correlated with oxy-Hb concentration changes in the mlOFC in response to gentle stroking touch.
source: Post-treatment OT concentration changes (30 min post-treatment and before task) were found to be positively correlated with pleasantness rating scores (Spearman's rho = 0.18, p=0.017) and oxy-Hb concentration changes in the mlOFC (Spearman's rho = 0.16, p=0.044) in response to the gentle stroking touch.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis between blood OT concentrations and neural responses.

claim: Post-treatment plasma OT concentration changes totally mediated the enhancement effects of intranasal OT on pleasantness ratings for gentle stroking touch.
source: By contrast, the results showed that post-treatment plasma OT concentration changes totally mediated the enhancement effects of intranasal (indirect effect = 0.42, SE = 0.166, 95% CI = [0.101, 0.768], bootstrap = 5000, Figure 6A) and oral OT (indirect effect = 0.15, SE = 0.071, 95% CI = [0.037, 0.310], bootstrap = 5000, Figure 6B) on pleasantness ratings.
evidence: This is a finding from mediation analysis, with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: Post-treatment plasma OT concentration changes totally mediated the enhancement effects of oral OT on pleasantness ratings for gentle stroking touch.
source: By contrast, the results showed that post-treatment plasma OT concentration changes totally mediated the enhancement effects of intranasal (indirect effect = 0.42, SE = 0.166, 95% CI = [0.101, 0.768], bootstrap = 5000, Figure 6A) and oral OT (indirect effect = 0.15, SE = 0.071, 95% CI = [0.037, 0.310], bootstrap = 5000, Figure 6B) on pleasantness ratings.
evidence: This is a finding from mediation analysis, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: Behavioral effects of both intranasally and orally administered OT were primarily mediated by peripheral changes in plasma OT concentrations following treatments.
source: Results from the model suggest that behavioral effects of both intranasally and orally administered OT were primarily mediated by peripheral changes in plasma OT concentrations following treatments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mediation analysis results.

claim: OT only facilitated behavioral and neural responses to gentle stroking touch, supporting the view that it is primarily influencing CT fiber mediated touch.
source: Our findings that OT only facilitated behavioral and neural responses to gentle stroking touch support the view that it is primarily influencing CT fiber mediated touch.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Similar functional effects of OT were produced after intranasal and oral administration, supporting the conclusion that the observed effects were primarily mediated by peripheral changes.
source: Here findings that similar functional effects of OT were produced after intranasal and oral administration, and that post-treatment changes in plasma OT concentrations significantly mediated behavioral effects, support the conclusion that the observed effects were primarily mediated by peripheral changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings comparing routes of administration.

claim: The facilitation of pSTS activity may reflect encoding of social components of the CT-targeted gentle stroking touch.
source: The facilitation of pSTS activity may thus reflect encoding of social components of the CT-targeted gentle stroking touch in line with the reported effects of intranasal and oral OT on social cognition and attention (Le et al., 2020; Le et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2018; Zhuang et al., 2021; Zhuang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural findings supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Individuals with autism or higher autistic traits tend to find light social touch as the most aversive.
source: Interestingly, individuals with autism or higher autistic traits tend to find light social touch as the most aversive (Ujiie and Takahashi, 2022) and this corresponds to reduced responses in both the OFC and STS (Kaiser et al., 2016; Voos et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Individuals with autism or higher autistic traits show reduced responses in both the OFC and STS to light social touch.
source: Interestingly, individuals with autism or higher autistic traits tend to find light social touch as the most aversive (Ujiie and Takahashi, 2022) and this corresponds to reduced responses in both the OFC and STS (Kaiser et al., 2016; Voos et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The main treatment effect of OT was to prolong the neural response to gentle-stroking touch rather than the magnitude of the initial response.
source: Plotting the time-course of responses in the mOFC and pSTS during gentle-stroking touch following OT treatment revealed that the main treatment effect was to prolong the neural response to the touch rather than the magnitude of the initial response.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the time-course analysis of neural data.

claim: OT may be acting to prolong the duration of the impact of the touch stimulation.
source: This may suggest that OT is acting to prolong the duration of the impact of the touch stimulation and possibly therefore facilitatory effects may have been even more pronounced for longer periods of touch.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the time-course findings.

claim: Facilitatory effects of OT may have been even more pronounced for longer periods of touch.
source: This may suggest that OT is acting to prolong the duration of the impact of the touch stimulation and possibly therefore facilitatory effects may have been even more pronounced for longer periods of touch.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the time-course findings.

claim: Some effects of exogenous OT treatment result from increased concentrations in the peripheral vascular system rather than following direct entry into the brain.
source: The finding in the current study that intranasal and oral administration of OT produced similar facilitation of behavioral and neural responses to gentle stroking touch provides further support for observations that some effects of exogenous treatment result from increased concentrations in the peripheral vascular system rather than following direct entry into the brain (Yao et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The intranasal administration route for OT produced significantly greater initial increases in plasma OT concentrations compared to an oral route.
source: Although, the intranasal administration route for OT produced significantly greater initial increases in plasma OT concentrations compared to an oral route in both the present study, and in two previous ones (Kou et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022), this did not result in significant route-dependent differences, possibly due to the high doses involved.
evidence: This is a finding from the blood sample analysis and comparison with previous studies.

claim: The greater initial increases in plasma OT concentrations from intranasal versus oral administration did not result in significant route-dependent functional differences, possibly due to the high doses involved.
source: Although, the intranasal administration route for OT produced significantly greater initial increases in plasma OT concentrations compared to an oral route in both the present study, and in two previous ones (Kou et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022), this did not result in significant route-dependent differences, possibly due to the high doses involved.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with a speculative explanation.

claim: The broadly similar functional effects of intranasal and oral OT in the context of behavioral and neural responses to gentle stroking touch are consistent with previous findings for visual attention toward social and non-social stimuli.
source: The broadly similar functional effects of intranasal and oral OT in the context of behavioral and neural responses to gentle stroking touch are also consistent with our previous findings for visual attention toward social and non-social stimuli (Zhuang et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022), although there is also evidence for route-dependent effects of OT on neural and behavioral effects on responses to emotional faces (Kou et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings with previous research by the authors.

claim: There is evidence for route-dependent effects of OT on neural and behavioral effects on responses to emotional faces.
source: The broadly similar functional effects of intranasal and oral OT in the context of behavioral and neural responses to gentle stroking touch are also consistent with our previous findings for visual attention toward social and non-social stimuli (Zhuang et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022), although there is also evidence for route-dependent effects of OT on neural and behavioral effects on responses to emotional faces (Kou et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Observed neural and behavioral effects of OT could be via it entering the brain by crossing the BBB and acting on its receptors in the OFC and pSTS as well as in other associated regions.
source: Thus, observed neural and behavioral effects of OT could be via it entering the brain by crossing the BBB and acting on its receptors in the OFC and pSTS as well as in other associated regions (Quintana et al., 2021; Quintana et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The effects of OT on neural and behavioral responses may be mediated via stimulation of vagal afferents to the brain via receptors in the heart and gastrointestinal system.
source: However, it is also possible that the effects of OT on neural and behavioral responses are mediated via stimulation of vagal afferents to the brain via receptors in the heart and gastrointestinal system (Carter, 2014; Carter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CT-targeted touch increased HRV (reflecting vagal activity) compared with rest.
source: In agreement with a previous study (Triscoli et al., 2017) we found that CT-targeted touch increased HRV (reflecting vagal activity) compared with rest.
evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Vagal stimulation can produce extensive activation in the brain, including in the frontal cortex and STS.
source: Vagal stimulation can also produce extensive activation in the brain, including in the frontal cortex and STS (Chae et al., 2003; Iseger et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: OT can influence both parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous system activity.
source: Studies have reported that OT can influence both parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous system activity (Kemp et al., 2012; de Oliveira et al., 2012), although in line with some other studies (Martins et al., 2020b; Yao et al., 2023) we did not observe any effects of intranasal or oral OT on SCR, heart rate or HRV during touch stimulation in the present study.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The current study did not observe any effects of intranasal or oral OT on SCR, heart rate or HRV during touch stimulation.
source: Studies have reported that OT can influence both parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous system activity (Kemp et al., 2012; de Oliveira et al., 2012), although in line with some other studies (Martins et al., 2020b; Yao et al., 2023) we did not observe any effects of intranasal or oral OT on SCR, heart rate or HRV during touch stimulation in the present study.
evidence: This is a finding from physiological data analysis.

claim: In rats, OT has been found to exert analgesic effects by influencing OT receptors in cutaneous nociceptive fibers in the dorsal route ganglion (C- and A-δ but not A-β fibers).
source: In rats, OT has been found to exert analgesic effects by influencing OT receptors in cutaneous nociceptive fibers in the dorsal route ganglion (C- and A-δ but not A-β fibers; González-Hernández et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Keratinocytes in the skin express OT receptors.
source: Keratinocytes in the skin also express OT receptors (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Deing et al., 2013) and can modulate responses of sensory neurons to touch (Talagas and Misery, 2019; Noguri et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Keratinocytes can modulate responses of sensory neurons to touch.
source: Keratinocytes in the skin also express OT receptors (Baumbauer et al., 2015; Deing et al., 2013) and can modulate responses of sensory neurons to touch (Talagas and Misery, 2019; Noguri et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The current study did not observe any indication that OT increased the sensitivity of CT fibers to touch given that only ratings of pleasantness were affected and not those of intensity.
source: However, in our current study we did not observe any indication that OT increased the sensitivity of CT fibers to touch given that only ratings of pleasantness were affected and not those of intensity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral rating findings.

claim: Behavioral and physiological indices of arousal in response to touch were unaffected by OT.
source: Behavioral and physiological indices of arousal in response to touch were also unaffected.
evidence: This is a finding from behavioral and physiological data analysis.

claim: CT fiber and non-CT fiber projections both to and within the brain are dissociable to some extent.
source: Since, CT fiber and non-CT fiber projections both to and within the brain are dissociable to some extent (Case et al., 2021; Marshall et al., 2019; McGlone et al., 2014) it is possible that the CT fiber projection system has more OT receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is possible that the CT fiber projection system has more OT receptors than the non-CT fiber system.
source: Since, CT fiber and non-CT fiber projections both to and within the brain are dissociable to some extent (Case et al., 2021; Marshall et al., 2019; McGlone et al., 2014) it is possible that the CT fiber projection system has more OT receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the differential effects of OT on different types of touch.

claim: fNIRS is restricted to measurement of changes in the superficial layers of the cortex and is unable to measure activity in deeper key touch, salience and reward processing regions.
source: Firstly, although using the well-established fNIRS technique made it easier to administer touch stimulation and take blood samples during brain activity recording it has inherent limitations in terms of being restricted to measurement of changes in the superficial layers of the cortex and being unable to measure activity in deeper key touch, salience and reward processing regions (McGlone et al., 2012; Pinti et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the fNIRS method supported by citations.

claim: Touch and massage interventions are increasingly demonstrated to have beneficial effects on brain development and function.
source: Touch and massage interventions are increasingly demonstrated to have beneficial effects on brain development and function and it is likely that their effects on OT release and signaling play a major role in this (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The effects of touch and massage interventions on OT release and signaling likely play a major role in their beneficial effects on brain development and function.
source: Touch and massage interventions are increasingly demonstrated to have beneficial effects on brain development and function and it is likely that their effects on OT release and signaling play a major role in this (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: OT treatment can facilitate behavioral and brain responses to gentle social touch/massage, which may have important translational therapeutic implications for using OT-based interventions in individuals with aberrant responses to social touch such as in autism.
source: Our findings demonstrating that OT treatment can facilitate behavioral and brain responses to gentle social touch/massage therefore may have important translational therapeutic implications for using OT-based interventions in individuals with aberrant responses to social touch such as in autism.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the translational implications of the findings.

claim: A 26-channel array consisting of 12 sources and 13 detectors were used to record hemodynamic activity of the bilateral lateral orbitofrontal cortex (lOFC), medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC), mediolateral orbitofrontal cortex (mlOFC), posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and the somatosensory area (S1).
source: A 26-channel array consisting of 12 sources and 13 detectors were used to record hemodynamic activity of the bilateral lateral orbitofrontal cortex (lOFC: channels 9, 18), medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC: channels 12–15) and mediolateral orbitofrontal cortex (mlOFC: channels 10, 11, 16, 17), posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS: channels 1–4, 23–26) and the somatosensory area (S1: channels 5–8, 19–22).
evidence: This is a description of the fNIRS recording setup, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The gentle touch and medium pressure massage were delivered on both legs simultaneously to control for possible preferences for left or right and more importantly to avoid unilateral brain activation.
source: The gentle touch and medium pressure massage were delivered on both legs simultaneously to control for possible preferences for left or right and more importantly to avoid unilateral brain activation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: For gentle touch, the masseur applied only a light stroking touch at the optimum velocity for activating CT fibers (5 cms/s) and at which subjects perceive this form of touch as most pleasant.
source: For gentle touch, the masseur applied only a light stroking touch at the optimum velocity for activating CT fibers (5 cms/s) and at which subjects perceive this form of touch as most pleasant (Löken et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: For the massage stimulation condition, the masseur applied a medium pressure massage moving discretely up and down the leg at the same velocity but without stroking the skin, designed to primarily target non-CT fibers.
source: For the massage stimulation condition, the masseur applied a medium pressure massage moving discretely up and down the leg at the same velocity but without stroking the skin, designed to primarily target non-CT fibers (Field, 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Participants were unable to guess better than chance whether they had received OT or PLC.
source: Participants were unable to guess better than chance whether they had received OT or PLC (χ2=0.43, p=0.512).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of blinding effectiveness.

claim: There were no significant differences in pleasantness ratings of the gentle stroking touch and medium pressure massage between the intranasal and oral PLC groups.
source: In line with our previous findings that oral and intranasal PLC administration do not produce different functional effects either at neural or behavioral levels (Kou et al., 2021; Zhuang et al., 2022), there were also no significant differences in pleasantness ratings of the gentle stroking touch and medium pressure massage between the intranasal and oral PLC groups (ps >0.110) confirming that knowledge of the route of administration had no effects.
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Knowledge of the route of administration had no effects on pleasantness ratings.
source: In line with our previous findings that oral and intranasal PLC administration do not produce different functional effects either at neural or behavioral levels (Kou et al., 2021; Zhuang et al., 2022), there were also no significant differences in pleasantness ratings of the gentle stroking touch and medium pressure massage between the intranasal and oral PLC groups (ps >0.110) confirming that knowledge of the route of administration had no effects.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that intranasal and oral PLC groups did not differ.

claim: The extraction efficiency of the OT assay was 96%.
source: Blood samples were analyzed in duplicate and a standard prior extraction step was performed following the recommended protocol from the manufacturers. Spiked samples (with 100 pg/ml OT added) were included with every assay to calculate extraction efficiency which was 96%.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the OT assay.

claim: The extraction step incorporated a fourfold concentration of samples using a vacuum concentrator resulting in a detection sensitivity of 2 pg/ml.
source: The extraction step incorporated a fourfold concentration of samples using a vacuum concentrator (Concentrator plus, Eppendorf, Germany) resulting in a detection sensitivity of 2 pg/ml.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the OT assay.

claim: All blood samples had detectable OT concentrations.
source: All samples had detectable concentrations.
evidence: This is a finding from the OT assay.

claim: The inter- and intra-assay coefficients of variation for the OT assay were 14% and 11% respectively.
source: The inter- and intra-assay coeﬃcients of variation were 14 and 11% respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the OT assay reliability.
